cases.query: What causes ocean tides?
contexts: Ocean tides result primarily from the differential gravitational acceleration exerted by the Moon (and to a lesser extent the Sun) across Earth's diameter. The near side of Earth experiences stronger lunar gravitational pull than the center of mass, which in turn experiences stronger pull than the far side. This creates two tidal bulges: one facing the Moon (direct gravitational attraction dominates) and one on the opposite side (centrifugal effect of the Earth-Moon barycentric orbit dominates). As Earth rotates through these bulges approximately every 24 hours and 50 minutes, most coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides per day. Spring tides occur during syzygy (new/full moon) when solar and lunar tidal forces align, while neap tides occur during quadrature (quarter moons) when they partially cancel.

Tides happen because the Moon pulls on Earth's water. The side of Earth closest to the Moon gets pulled harder, making the water bulge outward. Surprisingly, the opposite side also bulges because the Moon's pull is weakest there and the water gets left behind as Earth is pulled toward the Moon. As our planet spins, different coastlines rotate through these two bulges, giving most places two high tides a day. The Sun also pulls on our water but less strongly. When the Sun and Moon line up during full or new moons, tides are extra high and low. When they are at right angles during quarter moons, tides are more moderate.

Picture Earth's oceans as a stretchy rubber ball being squeezed between two hands from opposite sides. The Moon acts like a magnet pulling the rubber toward it on one side and allowing it to stretch away on the other side. As the ball rotates, every point on its surface passes through the stretched parts twice per rotation, experiencing two bulges per day. Now add a second, weaker magnet representing the Sun. When both magnets line up, the stretching is at its most extreme. When they pull at right angles, they partially fight each other, and the stretching is milder.
cases.description: Tidal mechanics explained via gravitational physics, simplified cause-effect, and rubber ball analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources agree: the Moon's differential gravitational pull creates two tidal bulges, Earth's rotation moves coastlines through them creating two daily tide cycles, and solar-lunar alignment modulates tide strength. The physics source mentions barycentric orbit, syzygy, and quadrature while the analogy uses 'rubber ball' and 'magnets.' The explanation is identical across all three despite zero shared technical terminology.

cases.query: How does a relational database ensure data consistency during concurrent transactions?
contexts: Relational databases enforce ACID properties through a combination of locking, logging, and isolation levels. Write-ahead logging (WAL) ensures durability by persisting changes to a sequential log before modifying data pages. Two-phase locking (2PL) prevents conflicting concurrent access: transactions acquire shared locks for reads and exclusive locks for writes, holding all locks until commit. Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC), used by PostgreSQL and Oracle, maintains multiple versions of each row so readers never block writers. Isolation levels (READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE) define visibility rules between concurrent transactions, with higher levels providing stronger consistency guarantees at the cost of reduced throughput.

When multiple users access a database at the same time, the database makes sure they do not interfere with each other. Before anyone modifies data, the database records what it plans to do in a journal. If the system crashes mid-change, the journal can undo incomplete work or redo lost work. The database also controls who can see what: one user's half-finished changes are invisible to others until they are complete and confirmed. Some databases keep old and new versions of data simultaneously so that people reading data are never forced to wait for someone who is writing data. The stricter you set these visibility rules, the more consistent the data but the slower things get.

Think of a relational database as a carefully managed library with strict checkout rules. Before a librarian changes anything in the catalog, they write what they plan to do on a sticky note. If the library loses power mid-update, they can use those sticky notes to restore everything. Two people cannot edit the same catalog card simultaneously. One must wait for the other to finish and put their card back. Some modern libraries keep photocopies of each card, so someone reading the old copy does not have to wait for the person rewriting the original. The library can set rules ranging from relaxed, where readers might see slightly outdated cards, to strict, where everyone always sees the most current version.
cases.description: Database concurrency control explained via ACID internals, simplified concepts, and library analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources describe the same mechanisms: write-ahead logging for crash recovery, locking or MVCC for concurrency, and isolation levels trading consistency for performance. The technical source references WAL, 2PL, and MVCC while the analogy uses 'sticky notes,' 'catalog cards,' and 'photocopies.' The concurrency control concepts are identical across all framings despite radically different vocabulary.

cases.query: How does the human kidney filter blood?
contexts: The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron, consisting of the glomerulus and renal tubule. Afferent arteriolar blood enters the glomerular capillary tuft at approximately 60 mmHg, where hydrostatic pressure drives ultrafiltration of plasma across the fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, and podocyte slit diaphragms. The resulting ultrafiltrate enters Bowman's capsule and flows through the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), where approximately 65% of sodium, water, and all glucose are reabsorbed via sodium-glucose linked transporters (SGLT2) and aquaporin channels. The loop of Henle establishes a corticomedullary osmotic gradient via countercurrent multiplication. The distal convoluted tubule (DCT) and collecting duct fine-tune electrolyte and water balance under hormonal control (aldosterone, ADH). The kidneys process approximately 180 liters of filtrate daily, producing 1-2 liters of concentrated urine.

Your kidneys clean your blood by pushing it through millions of tiny filters. Blood flows into these filters under pressure, which squeezes out water, salts, sugar, and waste products while keeping blood cells and large proteins in the bloodstream. The filtered fluid then travels through a long tube where the kidney reabsorbs almost everything useful, returning water, sugar, and essential salts back to the blood. Only the waste products and excess water continue on to become urine. Your kidneys filter your entire blood supply about 40 times per day, processing a huge volume but only producing a small amount of final urine because most of the water is reclaimed.

Imagine your kidney as a sophisticated water treatment plant. Raw water (blood) enters under pressure and is forced through a fine mesh screen (the glomerulus) that lets water and small dissolved substances through but blocks large debris (blood cells, proteins). The water then flows through a series of recovery channels. The first channel recovers most of the valuable minerals and nutrients. The middle section creates a special salt gradient that allows the plant to choose how concentrated the final waste water should be. The last section uses chemical signals from headquarters (hormones) to fine-tune exactly how much clean water to return to the city supply versus how much concentrated waste to send to the sewer.
cases.description: Kidney filtration explained via nephron physiology, patient-friendly language, and water treatment plant analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources describe the same filtration process: pressure-driven ultrafiltration in the glomerulus, selective reabsorption in the tubule, osmotic gradient creation in the loop of Henle, and hormonal fine-tuning in the distal segments. The physiology source references podocyte slit diaphragms, SGLT2 transporters, and countercurrent multiplication, while the analogy discusses 'mesh screens' and 'recovery channels.' The process described is identical; only the abstraction level changes.

cases.query: What is the legal doctrine of promissory estoppel?
contexts: Promissory estoppel, codified in Restatement (Second) of Contracts Section 90, provides an equitable remedy when a promisor makes a clear and definite promise, the promisee reasonably and foreseeably relies on that promise, the promisee suffers a substantial detriment as a result of the reliance, and injustice can only be avoided by enforcing the promise. Unlike traditional contract formation requiring consideration, promissory estoppel substitutes detrimental reliance for bargained-for exchange. Courts apply the doctrine when the promise induces action or forbearance of a definite and substantial character, and the remedy may be limited as justice requires rather than necessarily awarding full expectation damages. The burden of proof lies with the party asserting estoppel to demonstrate all four elements by a preponderance of evidence.

Promissory estoppel is a legal principle that protects people who reasonably relied on someone else's promise, even if there was no formal contract. If someone makes you a clear promise, you act on that promise in a way that changes your position, and it would be unfair to let them break the promise after you have already committed based on their word, a court can step in and hold them to it. The idea is that basic fairness should prevent people from making serious promises that lead others to take major actions and then walking away with no consequences. Courts will look at whether your reliance was reasonable and whether you genuinely suffered because of it.

Think of promissory estoppel as a legal safety net for broken promises. Normally, you need a formal deal with give-and-take on both sides for a promise to be enforceable. But sometimes one person makes a serious promise, and the other person takes a big leap of faith based on that promise, quitting their job, selling their house, or making a major investment. If the promisor then reneges, the law says it would be unjust to leave the person who relied on the promise holding the bag. The court can step in and either enforce the promise or award compensation for the losses caused by relying on it, even without a traditional contract.
cases.description: Promissory estoppel explained via legal doctrine, plain language, and practical metaphor
cases.rationale: All three sources describe identical legal elements: a clear promise, reasonable reliance, detrimental change of position, and injustice avoidable only by enforcement. The legal source cites Restatement Section 90 and discusses consideration substitution, while the practical version uses examples like quitting a job or selling a house. The doctrine described is the same across all three framings, but the vocabulary gap between legal terminology and everyday language would cause low similarity scores.

cases.query: How do neural networks learn from data?
contexts: Neural network training proceeds via stochastic gradient descent on a differentiable loss function. Forward propagation computes activations layer-by-layer: each neuron applies an affine transformation (z = Wx + b) followed by a nonlinear activation function (ReLU, sigmoid, or tanh). The loss function quantifies prediction error against ground truth labels. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute gradients of the loss with respect to each parameter. Weight updates follow the negative gradient direction scaled by a learning rate: w_new = w_old - lr * dL/dw. Regularization techniques including dropout, weight decay, and batch normalization prevent overfitting. Training continues for multiple epochs until convergence on a validation set.

Neural networks learn by repeatedly adjusting their internal settings. You feed the network examples with known answers, it makes predictions, and then it measures how wrong those predictions were. Based on that error measurement, the network figures out which of its settings contributed most to the mistake and nudges them in the direction that would reduce the error. This process repeats thousands or millions of times across the training data. Early on, predictions are essentially random, but gradually the adjustments accumulate and the network's predictions get closer and closer to the right answers. Extra techniques prevent the network from simply memorizing the training examples rather than learning general patterns.

Imagine a neural network as a new employee learning a job through feedback. Every day, the employee attempts tasks and a supervisor scores their work. The employee then reflects on what went wrong and adjusts their approach, focusing most on fixing the biggest mistakes. At first, performance is poor because adjustments are based on guesswork. But over weeks of daily practice and feedback, the employee develops reliable skills and intuition. The supervisor also makes sure the employee is learning transferable skills rather than just memorizing specific tasks by occasionally changing the examples and testing on new situations the employee has never seen.
cases.description: Neural network training described via calculus-based optimization, intuitive process, and employee training analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources describe the same learning process: forward pass prediction, error measurement, gradient-based parameter adjustment, iterative improvement, and regularization to prevent overfitting. The mathematical source discusses stochastic gradient descent and backpropagation while the analogy uses 'employee,' 'supervisor,' and 'feedback.' The training loop is identical in all three descriptions despite completely different framing and vocabulary.

cases.query: What is the principle behind how an MRI scanner produces images?
contexts: Magnetic resonance imaging exploits the quantum mechanical property of nuclear spin in hydrogen-1 protons. A superconducting magnet (typically 1.5T or 3T) polarizes the proton magnetic moments along the B0 field. Radiofrequency pulses at the Larmor frequency (42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen) tip the net magnetization vector into the transverse plane. During relaxation, precessing protons emit RF signals detected by receiver coils. T1 relaxation (spin-lattice) describes longitudinal magnetization recovery, while T2 relaxation (spin-spin) describes transverse signal decay. Gradient coils spatially encode signal via frequency and phase encoding. Fourier transformation of the raw k-space data produces the final image, with contrast determined by tissue-specific T1 and T2 relaxation times.

An MRI scanner uses a powerful magnet to temporarily align the hydrogen atoms in your body, which are abundant because your body is mostly water. Then it sends a brief radio wave pulse that knocks those atoms out of alignment. As the atoms snap back to their aligned state, they emit faint radio signals. Different tissues, fat versus muscle versus bone marrow, snap back at different speeds, and the scanner measures those differences. A computer processes the timing of all these signals to build a detailed picture of your internal organs without any radiation. The strong magnet is why you cannot bring metal into the MRI room.

Think of an MRI like conducting a census of an enormous stadium full of people. The powerful magnet makes everyone stand up and face the same direction. A loudspeaker (the radio pulse) then shouts a command that makes everyone sit down. Different sections of the stadium sit down at different speeds depending on what type of seat they are in: padded seats versus bleachers versus box seats. Detectors around the stadium record how quickly each section sits back down. By analyzing these timing patterns, a computer can create a map showing exactly where each type of seating is located, even seats hidden deep inside the stadium that you could never see from outside.
cases.description: MRI imaging principles described via nuclear physics, patient explanation, and stadium analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources describe the same imaging principle: magnetic alignment of hydrogen protons, RF excitation that disturbs alignment, tissue-specific relaxation signal measurement, and computational image reconstruction. The physics source discusses Larmor frequency and k-space while the analogy uses 'stadium' and 'seating sections.' Despite entirely different vocabulary, the physical process described is the same in each case.

cases.query: How does public key cryptography enable secure communication?
contexts: Public key cryptography relies on computationally asymmetric mathematical problems, typically the integer factorization problem (RSA) or the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDSA/ECDH). Each participant generates a key pair: a public key derived from the private key via a one-way trapdoor function. For encryption, the sender encrypts using the recipient's public key; only the corresponding private key can decrypt (IND-CPA security). For digital signatures, the signer produces a signature using their private key; anyone can verify using the corresponding public key, providing authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation. In practice, hybrid encryption is used: the sender generates a random symmetric key (AES-256), encrypts the message with it, then encrypts the symmetric key with the recipient's public key, achieving both efficiency and security.

Public key cryptography solves a fundamental problem: how can two people who have never met communicate securely? Each person creates two mathematically linked keys, one public and one private. You can share your public key with anyone. When someone wants to send you a secret message, they scramble it using your public key. The mathematical relationship between the keys is designed so that only your private key can unscramble it. Even if an eavesdropper intercepts the public key and the scrambled message, they cannot reverse the process without the private key. This also works for proving identity: you can use your private key to create a unique digital signature that anyone can verify with your public key but nobody can forge.

Imagine public key cryptography as a special mailbox. You install a mailbox with a slot that anyone can drop letters into (your public key) but only you have the key to open the mailbox door and retrieve them (your private key). Anyone in the world can send you a sealed letter through the slot, and only you can read it. For signing documents, imagine you have a unique rubber stamp that only you possess (private key) and everyone has a reference book showing what your stamp looks like (public key). When you stamp a document, anyone can check their reference book to confirm the stamp is genuine, but nobody can duplicate your stamp. In reality, sending the actual message through the mailbox slot is slow, so people usually just drop a regular padlock key through the slot and use that faster lock for the actual package.
cases.description: Public key cryptography explained via mathematical foundations, intuitive description, and mailbox/stamp analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources describe the same cryptographic system: asymmetric key pairs where the public key encrypts and the private key decrypts, digital signatures for authentication, and hybrid encryption for efficiency. The mathematical source discusses trapdoor functions and IND-CPA security while the analogy uses 'mailbox slots' and 'rubber stamps.' The security model is identical across all three despite completely different language, which would produce low pairwise similarity.

cases.query: How does the carbon cycle regulate atmospheric CO2?
contexts: The global carbon cycle operates through interconnected reservoirs and fluxes. Atmospheric CO2 is assimilated by terrestrial photosynthesis (gross primary production ~120 GtC/yr) and oceanic dissolution (~90 GtC/yr), governed by Henry's law and the carbonate buffering system (CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> HCO3- + H+ <-> CO3^2- + 2H+). Carbon returns to the atmosphere through autotrophic and heterotrophic respiration (~118 GtC/yr), ocean outgassing, volcanic degassing (~0.1 GtC/yr), and combustion of fossil fuels (~10 GtC/yr). Long-term sequestration occurs via marine sediment burial, silicate weathering consuming CO2 over millennial timescales, and lithification into carbonate rocks. The pre-industrial steady state maintained atmospheric CO2 at approximately 280 ppm. Anthropogenic emissions have disrupted this equilibrium, with natural sinks absorbing approximately 55% of annual emissions.

The carbon cycle is nature's way of recycling carbon between the air, land, and oceans. Plants pull CO2 out of the air during photosynthesis and build it into their tissues. When plants and animals die and decompose, or when living things breathe, that carbon goes back into the air. The ocean acts as a giant carbon sponge, absorbing CO2 from the atmosphere and dissolving it in seawater. Over very long time periods, carbon gets locked away in rocks and fossil fuels deep underground. Before humans started burning fossil fuels, the amount of carbon entering and leaving the atmosphere was roughly balanced. Now we are releasing stored underground carbon faster than nature can reabsorb it, causing CO2 levels to rise.

Think of the carbon cycle as a global banking system with carbon as the currency. The atmosphere is a checking account, the ocean is a savings account, and underground fossil fuels are a vault that has been locked for millions of years. Plants make regular deposits from the checking account into living biomass. Decomposition and breathing make withdrawals back to the checking account. The ocean savings account earns and pays interest slowly, absorbing and releasing carbon based on temperature and chemistry. For millennia, deposits and withdrawals balanced out. But humanity has been breaking into the ancient vault, burning fossil fuels, and dumping that long-stored carbon into the checking account faster than the savings account and plants can absorb the surplus.
cases.description: Carbon cycle regulation described via biogeochemistry, simplified ecology, and banking system analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources describe the same cycle: photosynthetic CO2 uptake, respiration/decomposition release, oceanic absorption, long-term geological sequestration, and anthropogenic disruption of the pre-industrial balance. The biogeochemistry source cites GtC/yr fluxes and carbonate buffering equations while the analogy uses 'checking accounts' and 'vaults.' Complete agreement on mechanism and disruption despite radically different framing that would yield low text similarity.

cases.query: How does a compiler transform source code into machine code?
contexts: Compilation proceeds through a multi-phase pipeline. Lexical analysis (scanning) tokenizes the source stream using finite automata, producing a token sequence. Syntactic analysis (parsing) constructs an abstract syntax tree (AST) using context-free grammar rules, typically via recursive descent or LALR(1) parsers. Semantic analysis performs type checking, scope resolution, and symbol table management. The intermediate representation (IR) phase generates platform-independent code, commonly static single assignment (SSA) form. Optimization passes operate on the IR: constant folding, dead code elimination, loop-invariant code motion, register allocation via graph coloring, and instruction scheduling. The backend code generator emits target-specific machine instructions, performs instruction selection via tree pattern matching, and produces relocatable object code linked into an executable binary.

A compiler translates human-readable programming code into the binary instructions that a processor can execute. It works in stages. First, it reads the code character by character and groups them into meaningful tokens like variable names, keywords, and operators. Then it checks whether these tokens are arranged in a grammatically correct structure, building a tree representation of the program. Next, it verifies that types match, variables are declared, and the logic makes sense. After that, it translates the validated program into a simpler internal format that is easier to improve. Various optimization steps make the program run faster or use less memory. Finally, it converts this optimized internal format into the specific machine instructions for your processor.

Think of a compiler as a translator turning a novel into a movie script in a foreign language. First, the translator reads the novel word by word and identifies sentences, paragraphs, and dialogue (tokenization). Then they diagram the sentence structure to understand the grammar (parsing). They check that characters referenced in chapter 10 were actually introduced earlier and that the plot is logically consistent (semantic analysis). Next, they create a simplified storyboard version that captures the essence without language-specific details (intermediate representation). The director then optimizes the storyboard, cutting unnecessary scenes, combining redundant shots, and rearranging sequences for better flow (optimization). Finally, the storyboard is translated into the specific foreign language with proper idioms and cultural references for the target audience (code generation).
cases.description: Compilation pipeline described through compiler theory, simplified stages, and novel-to-movie analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources describe the identical compilation pipeline: lexical analysis, parsing, semantic checking, IR generation, optimization, and code generation. The compiler theory source references SSA form, LALR(1) parsers, and graph coloring, while the analogy discusses 'novel,' 'storyboard,' and 'foreign language.' The pipeline stages map one-to-one across all three sources despite entirely different terminology.

cases.query: Why do airplanes generate lift?
contexts: Aerodynamic lift is generated through the interaction of an airfoil with the freestream airflow, governed by the Kutta-Joukowski theorem: L = rho * V * Gamma, where Gamma is the circulation around the airfoil. The asymmetric shape and positive angle of attack cause the flow to accelerate over the upper surface and decelerate below. By Bernoulli's principle (P + 0.5*rho*v^2 = constant along a streamline), higher velocity above produces lower static pressure, while lower velocity below produces higher static pressure, resulting in a net upward pressure differential. Simultaneously, Newton's third law perspective: the wing deflects the airstream downward (downwash), and the equal and opposite reaction is an upward force on the wing. Both descriptions are complementary views of the same phenomenon, and the Navier-Stokes equations provide the unified mathematical framework.

An airplane wing generates lift because of its shape and the angle at which it meets the air. The wing is curved more on top than on the bottom and tilted slightly upward. This combination forces air over the top of the wing to move faster than air underneath. Faster-moving air exerts less pressure, so the higher pressure underneath pushes the wing upward. At the same time, the wing pushes air downward as it moves forward, and the reaction to that push is an upward force on the wing. These two effects work together to keep the airplane aloft. The amount of lift depends on the wing's shape, its angle, the speed of the airplane, and the density of the air.

Think of an airplane wing as a hand sticking out of a car window. When you tilt your hand slightly upward, the wind catches the underside and pushes your hand up. That is basically what a wing does, but with a much more refined shape. The wing is sculpted so that air takes a longer, faster path over the top and a shorter, slower path underneath. The fast-moving air on top creates a partial vacuum that sucks the wing upward, while the slower air below pushes it upward from beneath. The wing is also subtly shoving air downward, and nature's rule that every push gets an equal push back means the air pushes the wing up in return.
cases.description: Lift generation explained via aerodynamic theory, simplified physics, and car window analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources identify the same lift mechanisms: pressure differential from asymmetric airflow (Bernoulli principle) and Newton's third law reaction from downwash. The aerodynamic source references Kutta-Joukowski theorem and Navier-Stokes equations while the analogy uses 'hand out of a car window' and 'partial vacuum.' The explanation is physically identical across all three despite different levels of mathematical formalism.

cases.query: How does a CDN improve website performance?
contexts: Content Delivery Networks improve web performance through geographic distribution of edge servers at Internet exchange points and ISP colocation facilities. Static assets are cached at edge nodes determined by BGP anycast routing, reducing round-trip time (RTT) by serving content from the nearest point of presence (PoP). TCP connection overhead is minimized through persistent connections between edge and origin, TLS session resumption, and HTTP/2 multiplexing. Dynamic content acceleration uses route optimization algorithms selecting paths with lowest latency and packet loss versus default BGP routes. Additional performance features include Brotli/gzip compression, image transcoding (WebP/AVIF), minification, HTTP/3 QUIC support for lossy networks, and edge computing capabilities for serverless function execution at the network edge. DDoS mitigation is achieved through distributed absorption of volumetric attacks across the CDN's aggregate bandwidth capacity.

A CDN makes websites faster by storing copies of the website's files on servers spread around the world. When someone visits the website, instead of connecting to a single distant server, they connect to whichever CDN server is geographically closest to them. This dramatically reduces the time it takes for data to travel back and forth. The CDN also compresses files to make them smaller, optimizes images for each visitor's device, and keeps connections ready so there is no setup delay. For content that changes frequently, the CDN finds the fastest route between its servers and the website's origin server rather than relying on the default internet path. As a bonus, spreading traffic across many servers makes the website harder to take down with denial-of-service attacks.

Imagine a CDN as a franchise restaurant chain compared to a single flagship restaurant. If there is only one restaurant in New York, every customer worldwide has to travel to New York to eat there, some waiting hours for their food to arrive by mail. A franchise puts restaurants in every major city, each serving the same menu from local kitchens. Customers get their food in minutes instead of hours. The franchise's central kitchen still prepares new menu items and special orders, but the standard dishes are already prepped at every location. If a mob shows up at one location trying to overwhelm it, the franchise can spread the crowd across all locations, preventing any single restaurant from being shut down.
cases.description: CDN performance benefits explained via network engineering, simplified web concepts, and restaurant franchise analogy
cases.rationale: All three sources describe the same CDN benefits: geographic distribution reduces latency, caching static content at edge locations, optimized routing for dynamic content, compression and optimization, and DDoS protection through distributed capacity. The networking source discusses BGP anycast, TLS session resumption, and QUIC while the analogy uses 'franchise restaurants' and 'local kitchens.' cases.query: What is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL?
contexts: PostgreSQL 16 Documentation, Chapter 13.2 - Transaction Isolation: The default transaction isolation level in PostgreSQL is Read Committed. In this mode, a SELECT query sees only data committed before the query began; it never sees uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during query execution. However, successive SELECT commands within a single transaction can see different data if other transactions commit changes between the two SELECTs. This differs from Repeatable Read, where all queries within a transaction see the same snapshot taken at the start of the first non-transaction-control statement.

Database administration handbook, section on concurrency: PostgreSQL ships with Read Committed as its default transaction isolation. This means each SQL statement within a transaction gets a fresh snapshot of the database. A practical implication: if transaction A reads a row, then transaction B updates and commits that row, then transaction A reads the same row again, transaction A will see B's changes on the second read. This is sometimes called 'non-repeatable read' and is permitted under Read Committed but prevented under Repeatable Read or Serializable isolation. To change the default for all sessions, set default_transaction_isolation in postgresql.conf.

Migration guide from MySQL to PostgreSQL: Both MySQL (InnoDB) and PostgreSQL default to different isolation levels. MySQL/InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read, while PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed. This difference can cause subtle behavioral changes when migrating applications. In PostgreSQL's Read Committed mode, concurrent writes never block reads, thanks to MVCC. Applications relying on MySQL's Repeatable Read semantics should explicitly set 'SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ' at the start of critical transactions, or adjust the server-wide default via the default_transaction_isolation parameter.

Troubleshooting guide for encoding issues: If you see garbled characters or 'invalid byte sequence' errors, the most common cause is a mismatch between the declared encoding and the actual file encoding. Solution: either convert your file to UTF-8, or add <?xml version='1.0' encoding='ISO-8859-1'?> at the top. Verify actual encoding with: file --mime-encoding document.xml.

contexts: Git Internals documentation: Git uses SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) to compute a 160-bit (40 hexadecimal character) hash for every object (blob, tree, commit, tag) stored in the repository. The hash is computed over a header (object type + content size + null byte) concatenated with the object content. This hash serves as the object's unique identifier and storage key in the object database (.git/objects/). As of Git 2.42, experimental support for SHA-256 (256-bit, 64 hex characters) is available via the --object-format=sha256 flag during git init, but SHA-1 remains the default and is used by all major hosting platforms including GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket.

Git Pro Book, Chapter 10: Every file and commit in a Git repository is checksummed with SHA-1 before it is stored, and the resulting 40-character hexadecimal hash becomes the reference to that content. This means Git is fundamentally a content-addressable filesystem. If even a single byte changes in a file, the entire hash changes, making it impossible to modify content without Git detecting it. The hash of a commit includes the hashes of its tree, parent commits, author, and message, creating an unbreakable chain of integrity from any commit back to the initial commit.

Security advisory, Git project (2024): While Git's default hashing algorithm, SHA-1, has known theoretical collision vulnerabilities (demonstrated by the SHAttered attack in 2017), Git implements the sha1dc (SHA-1 collision detection) library that detects and rejects known collision patterns. The Git project has been working on a transition plan to SHA-256 (documented in the hash function transition design document), with experimental support available since Git 2.29. However, the transition requires ecosystem-wide coordination, and SHA-1 remains the production default across all major Git implementations and hosting services as of 2024.
cases.description: Git's default hashing algorithm confirmed as SHA-1 across internals docs, Git Pro Book, and security advisory
cases.rationale: All three sources confirm Git uses SHA-1 as its default hashing algorithm. The internals documentation defines the mechanism, the Git Pro Book explains the content-addressable design, and the security advisory discusses known vulnerabilities while confirming SHA-1 remains the default. SHA-256 is mentioned as an experimental/future option in Sources A and C, but both explicitly state it is not the default. A classifier might flag the SHA-1/SHA-256 discussion as uncertainty about which algorithm is used, but the documentation is clear that SHA-1 is the current default.
